subtopics.name: Investigating The Rate of a Reaction

parts.problem_md:
**Procedure **

The student:

- uses a measuring cylinder to measure 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of dilute sulfuric acid
- adds the dilute sulfuric acid to a boiling tube
- sets up apparatus as shown in Fig. 3.1

![Diagram of gas collection: boiling tube with 10 cm³ dilute sulphuric acid and stopper, delivery tube into water trough, gas captured in inverted 25 cm³ cylinder](assets/001-diagram-of-gas-collection-boiling-tube-with-10-c.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

- removes the stopper from the boiling tube
- adds one spatula of metal F to the boiling tube
- puts the stopper back into the boiling tube and starts the stop-watch
- records in Table 3.1 the time taken to collect 5 cm<sup>3</sup> , 10 cm<sup>3</sup> , 15 cm<sup>3</sup> , 20 cm<sup>3</sup> and 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of gas.

(i) Fig. 3.2 shows the stop-watch readings for 5 cm<sup>3</sup> and 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of gas collected.

![Two digital timers show 10.04 s for 5 cm³ of gas and 56.61 s for 25 cm³ of gas, labelled with “min sec” under each display](assets/002-two-digital-timers-show-10-04-s-for-5-cm-of-gas-.png)

**Fig.3.2**

Record in Table 3.1 the time taken to the nearest second to collect 5 cm<sup>3</sup> and 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of gas.

**Table 3.1**

| volume of gas collected / cm³ | time taken / s |
|---|---|
| 5 |   |
| 10 | 22 |
| 15 | 34 |
| 20 | 46 |
| 25 |   |

[2]

(ii) State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.

[1]

(iii) On the grid, plot a graph of volume of gas collected (vertical axis) against time taken.

![Dense black-and-white grid of tiny uniform squares forming a full page of graph paper with thin lines and a narrow border around the edges](assets/003-dense-black-and-white-grid-of-tiny-uniform-squar.png)

[3]

(iv) Draw the line of best fit.

[1]

(v) Describe the relationship between the volume of gas collected and the time taken.

[1]

(vi) Suggest one possible source of error in the measurement of the time taken.

[1]

(vii) Suggest one way to obtain a more accurate measurement of the volume of gas collected.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) 10 (s) and 57 (s) **[1 mark each]**
> - (ii) Independent variable: volume of gas collected; dependent variable: time taken **[1 mark]**
> - (iii) Axes correct way round, labelled with quantity and unit; suitable linear scales; points plotted correctly **[3 marks]**
> - (iv) Line of best fit drawn **[1 mark]**
> - (v) As the volume of gas collected increases, the time taken increases (or reverse) **[1 mark]**
> - (vi) A source of error, e.g. difficulty watching both volume and stop-watch at once, or delay starting timing **[1 mark]**
> - (vii) A way to improve accuracy, e.g. use a gas syringe **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept quicker rate of bubbles/more effervescence; x-axis time/s, y-axis volume of gas/cm<sup>3</sup>; ecf from (b)(i); accept ± ½ small square; ecf from (b)(iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reading stop-watch displays to the nearest second is a common source of small errors — always double-check whether the display shows minutes and seconds separately before recording your value.

parts.problem_md:
**Procedure**

- Set up the apparatus as shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Diagram of gas collection: boiling tube with stopper connected by delivery tube to inverted 25 cm³ measuring cylinder over water in a trough, held by clamp.](assets/004-diagram-of-gas-collection-boiling-tube-with-stop.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

- Use the 10 cm<sup>3 </sup>measuring cylinder to measure 10 cm<sup>3 </sup>of dilute sulfuric acid.
- Remove the stopper from the boiling tube.
- Add the dilute sulfuric acid to the boiling tube.
- Add about 1 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous copper(II) sulfate to the boiling tube.
- Add a spatula of metal **F** to the boiling tube.
- Put the stopper back into the boiling tube and start the stop-watch.

(i) Record in Table 3.1 the time taken to collect 5 cm<sup>3</sup> , 10 cm<sup>3</sup> , 15 cm<sup>3</sup> , 20 cm<sup>3</sup> and 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of gas.

Record each time to the nearest second.

**Table 3.1**

| volume of gas collected  / cm<sup>3</sup> | time taken  / s |
|---|---|
| 5 |   |
| 10 |   |
| 15 |   |
| 20 |   |
| 25 |   |

[3]

(ii) State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.

independent variable ......................................................................................................... dependent variable ............................................................................................................

[1]

(iii) On the grid, plot a graph of volume of gas collected (vertical axis) against time taken.

![Square sheet of fine graph paper with dense, evenly spaced black grid lines forming many small squares across the entire white page](assets/005-square-sheet-of-fine-graph-paper-with-dense-even.png)

[3]

(iv) Draw the line of best fit.

[1]

(v) Describe the relationship between the volume of gas collected and the time taken.

[1]

(vi) Suggest one possible source of error in the measurement of the time taken.

[1]

(vii) Suggest one way to obtain a more accurate measurement of the volume of gas collected.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) Five times recorded, increasing down the table, all to the nearest second **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Independent variable: volume of gas collected; dependent variable: time taken **[1 mark]**
> - (iii) Axes the correct way round, labelled with quantity and unit; suitable linear scales so plots cover more than half the grid; points plotted correctly **[3 marks]**
> - (iv) Line of best fit drawn **[1 mark]**
> - (v) As the volume of gas collected increases, the time taken increases (or reverse argument) **[1 mark]**
> - (vi) A source of error, e.g. difficulty watching both the volume and stop-watch at once, or delay starting the stop-watch **[1 mark]**
> - (vii) A way to improve accuracy, e.g. use a gas syringe, or keep reactants separate until ready to start timing **[1 mark]**
> 
> x-axis is time / s and y-axis is volume (of gas collected) / cm<sup>3</sup>; accept ± ½ small square; ecf from (b)(i) and (iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When plotting rate-of-reaction graphs, always check your scale uses more than half the grid in both directions — a common mark loss is a technically correct but cramped graph.

parts.problem_md:
Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce calcium chloride.

(i) State the names of the other **two** products in this reaction.

[2]

(ii) The rate of this reaction can be increased by increasing the temperature of the hydrochloric acid.

Explain why.

Use ideas about particle collisions and energy in your answer.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) Carbon dioxide **[1 mark]**
> - (i) Water **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Frequency of collisions increases **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) More particles have kinetic energy greater than the activation energy / collisions are more energetic / more collisions are successful **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining rate increases with temperature, always mention BOTH more frequent collisions AND more successful (higher-energy) collisions — one alone only earns partial credit.

parts.problem_md:
Iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form hydrogen and a salt.

(i) Explain why this is a chemical change.

[1]

(ii) State the test for hydrogen and give the observation for a positive result.

test .................................................

observation .....................................

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) A new substance is made **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Test: lighted splint; result: burns with a squeaky pop **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> "A new substance formed" is the key phrase examiners look for when justifying a chemical (not physical) change — a colour or state change alone isn't enough.

parts.problem_md:
Iron is used as a catalyst in some chemical reactions.

Describe what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - A substance that increases the rate of a reaction **[1 mark]**
> - Is unchanged at the end of the reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both parts of the definition are needed for full marks — stating only "speeds up a reaction" without "unchanged at the end" will lose a mark.

parts.problem_md: Which statement explains how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
- This means more colliding particles have sufficient energy to react, increasing the rate of reaction

**A** is incorrect because a catalyst does not change the energy of the particles in the reaction mixture

**B** is incorrect because a catalyst reduces, not increases, the minimum energy particles need to react

**C** is incorrect because a catalyst does not change the energy of the particles in the reaction mixture

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: It increases the energy of the particles in the reaction mixture.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: It increases the minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: It reduces the energy of the particles in the reaction mixture.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: It reduces the minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react.
